items.title: Babur & the Foundation of the Mughal Empire (1526-1530)
items.body:
**In one line:** Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire by winning the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

**The story**

- **Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur** (born 1483 at Andijan in Ferghana) was a **descendant of Timur** (father's side) and **Genghis/Chinggis Khan** (mother's side), so he inherited the Timurid claim.
- After losing his Central Asian homelands (Samarqand, Ferghana), he captured **Kabul in 1504** and used it as a base to march into Hindustan.
- At **Panipat (1526)**, though heavily outnumbered, he beat Ibrahim Lodi using **field artillery** and the Ottoman (Rumi) **tulughma / linked-cart** tactic he had learnt about from the battle of Chaldiran (1514).
- Three more wins secured north India; he died at Agra in **1530** and was succeeded by his son **Humayun**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The founder, the four battles with years, Babur's lineage and the Baburnama are the standard Prelims facts for Mughal origins.

**Picture it — the four decisive battles**

| Battle | Year | Opponent | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First Panipat** | 1526 | Ibrahim Lodi (Delhi Sultan) | Ended the Lodi/Delhi Sultanate; founded Mughal rule |
| **Khanwa** | 1527 | Rana Sanga (Mewar) | Broke the Rajput confederacy; consolidated N. India |
| **Chanderi** | 1528 | Medini Rai (Malwa) | Captured Chanderi (Rajputs performed jauhar) |
| **Ghaghra** | 1529 | Afghan confederacy | Secured the east (Bihar/Bengal frontier) |

**Terms explained**

- **Timurid** = descended from Timur (Tamerlane), the 14th-century Central Asian conqueror.
- **tulughma / linked-cart (araba)** = tying carts together with gaps for guns, making a mobile shield-wall; artillery fires through the gaps.
- **jauhar** = Rajput practice of mass self-immolation by women to avoid capture.
- **Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi)** = Babur's own memoirs, written in **Chagatai Turkish**.
- **Charbagh** = a four-part Persian garden (Babur's Aram Bagh / Ram Bagh at Agra).

**Don't confuse:** The **First** Battle of Panipat (1526, Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi) with the **Second** (1556, Akbar's regent Bairam Khan vs Hemu) and the **Third** (1761, Marathas vs Ahmad Shah Abdali) — three different battles on the same field.

**Remember it:** Babur's battles "P-K-C-G" = Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghra (1526-27-28-29).

**TL;DR**

- Babur, descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.
- First Panipat (1526) ended the Delhi Sultanate; Khanwa (1527), Chanderi (1528), Ghaghra (1529) followed.
- He used artillery and the tulughma (linked-cart) tactic to beat larger armies.
- Wrote the Baburnama in Chagatai Turkish; introduced Charbagh gardens; died 1530.
keyPoints: Babur, descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.
First Battle of Panipat (1526) defeated Ibrahim Lodi and ended the Delhi Sultanate.
Battle of Khanwa (1527) defeated Rana Sanga; Chanderi (1528) and Ghaghra (1529) followed.
Babur used artillery and the tulughma (linked-cart) tactic to beat larger armies.
He wrote the Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi) in Chagatai Turkish and introduced Charbagh gardens.

items.title: Humayun & the Sur Interregnum (Sher Shah Suri)
items.body:
**In one line:** Humayun lost the throne to the brilliant Afghan administrator Sher Shah Suri, spent 15 years in exile, and won it back in 1555 — just before dying.

**The story**

- **Humayun** (ruled 1530-40, then 1555-56) weakened himself early by **dividing the empire among his brothers** (Kamran, Askari, Hindal).
- The Afghan **Sher Shah Suri** beat him at **Chausa (1539)** and **Kannauj/Bilgram (1540)**; Humayun fled into **15 years of exile in Safavid Persia**, sheltered by **Shah Tahmasp**.
- Sher Shah then ruled for just five years (**1540-45**) but reformed revenue, coinage and roads so effectively that Humayun himself called him **'Ustad-i-Badshahan' (Teacher of Kings)**. His work became the **base for Akbar's administration** and later British revenue systems.
- Humayun **recaptured Delhi in 1555** (battles of Machhiwara and Sirhind) and died in **1556** after a fall from his library stairs. His widow built **Humayun's Tomb** — India's **first garden tomb** and a model for the Taj Mahal.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Sher Shah's reforms (rupiya, GT Road, patta/kabuliyat) are among the most-asked administrative facts of the whole medieval syllabus.

**Picture it — Sher Shah's reforms**

| Area | Reform |
|---|---|
| Revenue | sarkars → parganas; land measured & classified; state share **one-third**; **patta** (title deed) + **kabuliyat** (agreement) |
| Coinage | standardised the **silver rupiya** and **copper dam** |
| Roads | restored the **Grand Trunk Road** with **sarais** (inns) |
| Military | revived **dagh** (branding horses) and **chehra** (soldier roll) from Alauddin Khalji |

**Terms explained**

- **interregnum** = a gap between two spells of one dynasty's rule (here the Sur rule between Humayun's two reigns).
- **patta** = a document stating a peasant's holding and dues; **kabuliyat** = the peasant's written agreement to pay.
- **sarai** = a roadside inn for travellers and traders.
- **rupiya** = Sher Shah's silver coin, ancestor of today's rupee.

**Don't confuse:** **Sher Shah Suri** (Afghan, Sur dynasty) was *not* a Mughal — he interrupted Mughal rule. **Humayun's Tomb** (first garden tomb) is distinct from the later Taj Mahal it inspired.

**Remember it:** Sher Shah = "RRR" — Rupiya, Roads (GT Road), Revenue reforms.

**TL;DR**

- Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), then was exiled to Safavid Persia.
- He recaptured Delhi in 1555 and died in 1556; Humayun's Tomb is India's first garden tomb.
- Sher Shah Suri (Farid Khan) founded the Sur dynasty and ruled 1540-45.
- His reforms — rupiya, GT Road, patta/kabuliyat, dagh & chehra — became the base for Akbar's administration.
keyPoints: Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), then exiled to Safavid Persia.
He recaptured Delhi in 1555 and died in 1556; Humayun's Tomb is India's first garden tomb.
Sher Shah Suri (Farid Khan) founded the Sur dynasty and ruled 1540-45.
Sher Shah's revenue: sarkar/pargana units, one-third produce, patta and kabuliyat to peasants.
He introduced the silver rupiya and copper dam, revived the Grand Trunk Road with sarais, and used dagh & chehra.

items.title: Akbar the Great (1556-1605): Conquests, Religion & Administration
items.body:
**In one line:** Akbar (ruled 1556-1605) built the Mughal Empire's lasting strength by combining military conquest, religious tolerance, and systematic administration.

**The story**

- **Jalal-ud-din Akbar** came to the throne aged 13 in **1556** under the regent **Bairam Khan**, who won the **Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** against **Hemu**.
- He expanded through campaigns such as the **Siege of Chittorgarh (1567-68)**, **Haldighati (1576)** against **Maharana Pratap** (Mughal army led by **Man Singh**), and the annexation of **Gujarat (1573)** and **Bengal (1576)**.
- In religion he abolished the **jizya**, promoted **Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace)**, debated faiths at the **Ibadat Khana**, and founded the syncretic **Din-i-Ilahi (1582)** (few followers).
- For administration he built two famous systems — the **Dahsala/Zabti** revenue system (with **Raja Todar Mal**) and the **Mansabdari** rank system — that bound nobles to the emperor and gave the treasury stability.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Mansabdari (Zat/Sawar), Dahsala, Sulh-i-Kul, Din-i-Ilahi and the Navaratnas are among the highest-frequency Mughal exam points.

**Picture it — Akbar's two key systems**

| System | What it did |
|---|---|
| **Dahsala / Zabti** (Todar Mal's Bandobast) | Revenue fixed on the **average produce & prices of 10 years**; state share one-third. Alternatives: Batai/Ghalla-Bakshi, Kankut |
| **Mansabdari** | Every officer held a **mansab (rank)** with two numbers — **Zat** (personal status/pay) and **Sawar** (cavalry to maintain); ranks 10 up to 5,000 (7,000 for princes) |

**Terms explained**

- **jizya** = a tax that had been levied on non-Muslims; Akbar abolished it.
- **Sulh-i-Kul** = "peace with all", Akbar's policy of treating all religions equally.
- **Din-i-Ilahi** = Akbar's blended "religion of God" (1582), drawing from several faiths.
- **Zat / Sawar** = the two numbers of a mansab — Zat = rank/status, Sawar = number of horsemen to keep.
- **Navaratnas** = Akbar's "nine gems" (notably **Todar Mal, Abul Fazl, Tansen, Birbal, Man Singh, Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, Faizi**); **Abul Fazl** wrote the **Akbarnama**, whose third volume is the **Ain-i-Akbari**.

**Don't confuse:** **Zat vs Sawar** — Zat is personal status, Sawar is the cavalry quota. The **Akbarnama** is the history; its **third volume**, the **Ain-i-Akbari**, is the administrative gazetteer.

**Remember it:** Mansab pair = "Zat = self, Sawar = soldiers (horses)."

**TL;DR**

- Akbar acceded 1556; Bairam Khan won Second Panipat against Hemu.
- Conquests: Chittorgarh (1567-68), Haldighati (1576), Gujarat (1573), Bengal (1576).
- Religion: abolished jizya, promoted Sulh-i-Kul, founded Din-i-Ilahi (1582).
- Dahsala/Zabti fixed revenue on 10-year averages; Mansabdari ranks had Zat and Sawar; Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama (Ain-i-Akbari).
keyPoints: Akbar acceded in 1556; Bairam Khan won the Second Battle of Panipat against Hemu.

Dahsala/Zabti (Todar Mal's Bandobast) fixed revenue on 10-year average produce, one-third share.
Mansabdari ranks had Zat (status) and Sawar (cavalry) components.
Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama; its third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari.

items.title: Jahangir & Shah Jahan: Nur Jahan, English Contact & the Architectural Peak
items.body:
**In one line:** Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan the Mughal court reached its cultural and architectural peak — Nur Jahan's political power, the first English contacts, and the Taj Mahal all belong here.

**The story**

- Prince **Salim** took the title **Jahangir** ("world-seizer") in **1605**. In 1611 he married **Mehr-un-Nisa (Nur Jahan)**, whose faction (the "Nur Jahan Junta") dominated the court.
- English contact grew: Captain Hawkins visited, **Sir Thomas Roe** (envoy of James I, 1615-19) secured trading rights, and the English set up their **first factory at Surat (1613)**. Jahangir lost **Qandahar** to Persia (1622) and was known for the **Zanjir-i-Adl (chain of justice)** at Agra Fort.
- Prince **Khurram**, titled **Shah Jahan** (ruled **1628-1658**), built the **Taj Mahal** for **Mumtaz Mahal (Arjumand Banu)**, who died in 1631. His reign is the **golden age of Mughal architecture**.
- When he fell ill in 1657, a **war of succession** broke out among his sons; **Aurangzeb** won and imprisoned him in **Agra Fort** until his death in **1666**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Nur Jahan, Thomas Roe/Surat 1613, the Taj Mahal and the Peacock Throne are repeated match and date questions.

**Picture it**

| Ruler | Reign | Remember for |
|---|---|---|
| Jahangir (Salim) | 1605-1627 | Nur Jahan; Thomas Roe & Surat factory (1613); chain of justice |
| Shah Jahan (Khurram) | 1628-1658 | Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Peacock Throne |

**Terms explained**

- **Zanjir-i-Adl** = a "chain of justice" with bells, which any subject could pull to seek the emperor's hearing.
- **factory** = a fortified trading warehouse of the East India Company (not a modern mill).
- **Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus)** = Shah Jahan's jewelled imperial throne.
- **Mumtaz Mahal** = Shah Jahan's queen (Arjumand Banu); the Taj Mahal is her tomb.

**Don't confuse:** **Jahangir = Prince Salim; Shah Jahan = Prince Khurram.** The **first English factory (Surat, 1613)** came slightly *before* Thomas Roe's embassy (1615-19), which then won formal trading rights.

**Remember it:** "Salim → Jahangir → Nur Jahan; Khurram → Shah Jahan → Taj Mahal."

**TL;DR**

- Jahangir (Prince Salim) married Nur Jahan (1611), who held major political influence.
- Sir Thomas Roe secured trading rights; the English set up their first factory at Surat in 1613.
- Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal and the Peacock Throne — the architectural golden age.
- Aurangzeb won the war of succession and imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort till 1666.

items.title: Aurangzeb & the Decline of the Mughal Empire
items.body:
**In one line:** The empire reached its largest size under Aurangzeb, but his religious orthodoxy, endless Deccan wars, and later weak successors led to rapid decline.

**The story**

- **Aurangzeb Alamgir** (ruled **1658-1707**) won a **war of succession** against **Dara Shikoh**, imprisoned Shah Jahan, and ruled as an orthodox Sunni nicknamed **'Zinda Pir' (living saint)**.
- His **religious measures** — re-imposing **jizya in 1679**, appointing **muhtasibs (moral police)**, ending court music, and executing **Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675)** — alienated Hindus, Rajputs and Sikhs.
- In the **Deccan** he annexed **Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87)** — bringing Andhra's Qutb Shahi Golconda under Mughal rule — but decades of costly war against the **Marathas (Shivaji, Sambhaji)** drained the treasury (the "Deccan ulcer"). The empire reached its **greatest extent** yet was overstretched. He died at **Ahmednagar in 1707**.
- Afterwards, weak successors became **puppets of nobles**; the empire fractured.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The "peak-yet-decline" paradox, jizya 1679, Nadir Shah 1739 and the break-away provinces are classic Prelims and Mains material.

**Picture it — causes of decline**

| Type | Factors |
|---|---|
| Aurangzeb's policies | jizya (1679), orthodoxy, Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution, the Deccan ulcer |
| Structural | empty treasury, jagirdari crisis, Irani-Turani factionalism, weak successors |
| External shocks | **Nadir Shah** sacked Delhi (**1739, Battle of Karnal**), took the Peacock Throne & Koh-i-Noor; **Ahmad Shah Abdali** raided 1748-61 |
| Break-away provinces | Hyderabad (Asaf Jahi/Nizam), Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan), Awadh |

**Terms explained**

- **jizya** = the tax on non-Muslims that Akbar had abolished and Aurangzeb re-imposed in 1679.
- **muhtasib** = an official enforcing public morality and Islamic law.
- **jagirdari crisis** = too many nobles competing for too few revenue-assignment lands (jagirs).
- **Sayyid Brothers** = powerful nobles who made and unmade later emperors ("king-makers").

**Don't confuse:** Aurangzeb's reign was the empire's **largest in area** but the **start of its decline** — size did not mean strength. **Bahadur Shah II** (the last Mughal) was exiled after the **1857 Revolt**, long after real power had gone.

**Remember it:** Aurangzeb = peak size but "Deccan ulcer" + jizya (1679) = seed of decline.

**TL;DR**

- Aurangzeb won the succession war against Dara Shikoh; called Zinda Pir.
- Re-imposed jizya (1679), used muhtasibs, executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675).
- Annexed Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87) but exhausted the empire in Deccan/Maratha wars; died 1707.
- Nadir Shah sacked Delhi (1739); provinces (Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh) broke away; Bahadur Shah II exiled after 1857.
keyPoints: Aurangzeb won the war of succession against Dara Shikoh; called Zinda Pir.
He re-imposed jizya in 1679, appointed muhtasibs, and executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675).
Annexed Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87) but exhausted the empire in Deccan/Maratha wars; died 1707.
Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739 (Battle of Karnal), taking the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor.
Later Mughals were puppets of nobles like the Sayyid Brothers; provinces (Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh) broke away.
Bahadur Shah II, the last Mughal, was exiled to Rangoon after the 1857 Revolt.

items.title: The Marathas: Shivaji & the Peshwas
items.body:
**In one line:** The Marathas, led first by Chhatrapati Shivaji and later by the Peshwas, rose as the great power that challenged and outlasted the Mughals in the Deccan.

**The story**

- **Chhatrapati Shivaji** (1630-1680), born at **Shivneri Fort** and inspired by his mother **Jijabai** and guardian **Dadoji Kondadeo**, coined the ideal of **'Hindavi Swarajya'** (self-rule).
- He rose against **Bijapur** — killing **Afzal Khan** at **Pratapgarh (1659)** — raided **Surat (1664)**, signed the **Treaty of Purandar (1665)** with Jai Singh, and escaped from Agra (1666).
- Crowned **Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674**, he was a master of **guerrilla warfare**, held hundreds of forts, built a navy, and ran the state through the **Ashtapradhan** (council of eight ministers). He levied **Chauth** (one-fourth of revenue) and **Sardeshmukhi** (an extra one-tenth) on neighbouring lands.
- After Shivaji and **Sambhaji** (executed by Aurangzeb, 1689), real power passed to the **Peshwas**: **Shahu** appointed **Balaji Vishwanath** Peshwa in **1713**. The Marathas expanded until the disastrous **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)** loss to **Ahmad Shah Abdali**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Shivaji's coronation, Ashtapradhan, Chauth/Sardeshmukhi and Panipat 1761 are high-frequency facts and link directly to Mughal decline.

**Picture it — Maratha landmarks**

| Event | Year |
|---|---|
| Killed Afzal Khan (Pratapgarh) | 1659 |
| Raided Surat | 1664 |
| Treaty of Purandar | 1665 |
| Crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad | 1674 |
| Balaji Vishwanath made Peshwa | 1713 |
| Third Battle of Panipat (vs Abdali) | 1761 |

**Terms explained**

- **Hindavi Swarajya** = Shivaji's idea of self-rule for the people of the land.
- **Ashtapradhan** = Shivaji's "council of eight" ministers, headed by the **Peshwa** (prime minister).
- **Chauth** = a tax of one-fourth of revenue; **Sardeshmukhi** = an extra one-tenth, levied on lands outside the kingdom.
- **Peshwa** = the Maratha prime minister; after 1713 the Peshwas became the real rulers.

**Don't confuse:** **Chauth = 1/4, Sardeshmukhi = extra 1/10** (not the other way round). The **Third** Panipat (1761) was Marathas vs Abdali — not Babur or Akbar.

**Remember it:** Maratha taxes = "Chauth = 1/4, Sardeshmukhi = extra 1/10."

**TL;DR**

- Shivaji coined 'Hindavi Swarajya' and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674.
- He killed Afzal Khan at Pratapgarh (1659), raided Surat (1664), signed the Treaty of Purandar (1665).
- Ashtapradhan was his council of eight ministers headed by the Peshwa; Chauth (1/4) and Sardeshmukhi (extra 1/10) were the taxes.
- Shahu made Balaji Vishwanath Peshwa in 1713; the Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) to Abdali.

The Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) to Ahmad Shah Abdali.

items.title: For Mains — The Mughal Empire
items.body:
**In one line:** For APPSC Mains Paper-II (medieval India — Mughal administration and culture, Shivaji & the Marathas), the Mughals are the model empire for analysing statecraft, religious policy and the causes of imperial decline.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Administration | Mansabdari (Zat/Sawar), Dahsala/Zabti revenue, Sher Shah's foundations, provincial structure |
| Religious policy | Akbar's Sulh-i-Kul & Din-i-Ilahi vs Aurangzeb's jizya (1679) and orthodoxy — tolerance as statecraft |
| Culture | Indo-Persian synthesis: architecture (Taj, Red Fort), painting, language, Akbarnama/Ain-i-Akbari |
| Economy | Land-revenue as the fiscal base; the jagirdari crisis; trade and the first European factories |
| Significance | Longest-lasting pan-Indian empire; administrative template inherited by the British |
| Decline / criticism | Multi-causal: Deccan ulcer, fiscal exhaustion, factionalism, weak successors, external shocks |

**Data points / names / reports to quote**

- **1526** Panipat; **1556-1605** Akbar; **1679** jizya re-imposed; **1686-87** Bijapur-Golconda annexed; **1707** Aurangzeb's death; **1739** Nadir Shah; **1761** Panipat III.
- **Abul Fazl's Akbarnama / Ain-i-Akbari**; **Todar Mal's** Dahsala; **Sher Shah** as 'Ustad-i-Badshahan'.
- Historiography: the debate on Mughal decline (Satish Chandra's jagirdari crisis; Irfan Habib on the agrarian crisis).

**The AP angle:** Aurangzeb's **annexation of Golconda (1687)** brought the Telugu Qutb Shahi country under the Mughals; the region soon passed to the **Asaf Jahi Nizams of Hyderabad** — a vivid local illustration of imperial overreach.

**Use in answers**

- Example: contrast Akbar's inclusive consolidation with Aurangzeb's orthodoxy to argue that legitimacy, not territory, held the empire together.
- Quote: Humayun's tribute to Sher Shah as 'Teacher of Kings' to open an administration answer.
- Diagram idea: a cause-tree for Mughal decline (policy / structural / external branches).
keyPoints: Mains Paper-II clause (M2-3): Mughal administration & culture; Shivaji & the Marathas.
Frame administration-religion-culture-economy-significance-decline.
Cite Akbarnama/Ain-i-Akbari, Todar Mal's Dahsala, and the decline-debate historiography.
AP angle: Golconda's 1687 annexation and the rise of the Asaf Jahi Nizams of Hyderabad.
